summary:
Neuquén Province stands under Argentina's national framework. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

No Neuquén-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented, so what a visitor faces runs through national instruments rather than through any provincial trans regime.

The decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Violence risk is documented at national scale. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina during 2025, a record and a 62% rise year-on-year, averaging one every 38 hours and the worst of the observatory's ten years. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 of 227); 64.8% of cases (147) involved physical violence against bodily integrity. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers acting in public space, with beatings the main modality.

Activists interviewed in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. They report that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed.

Protection machinery exists on paper: Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections run through national and provincial laws. Against that, the national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry was eliminated and trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law were dismissed, with activists saying the quota is no longer implemented, which narrows the route to official redress.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute, so the gap between the text of Law 26.743 and its day-to-day operation has widened. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration against a statute that still stands.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. Agencia Presentes reported the observatory's figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, attributing the surge to the government's 'cultural battle' and hate discourse. The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands. Hate-crime charges in comparable cases therefore turn on the ordinary aggravators rather than on a gender-motivation finding.
localsOnly:
Residents change legal gender through an administrative route with no surgery, hormone treatment or court order required, and the 'X' option on the national DNI has been open since 2021.

The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans people; trans hires made under it were dismissed and activists say the measure is no longer being implemented. The national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry has been eliminated, removing the ministry that had administered much of this policy area.

For resident minors, the decree of 5 February 2025 restricts access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy. DNU 62/2025 covers minors' gender-affirming treatments in the same period. Transgender people in custody are governed by a separate decree on prison housing.

Anti-discrimination protections that residents rely on come from national and provincial law rather than from any Neuquén trans statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation challenging the February 2025 decree on minors is not recorded in the sources available here; the petition and the legal experts' position are documented, the ruling is not.

No Neuquén-specific enforcement data, incident series or provincial trans statute is sourced. That gap is not evidence of absence: most Argentine provinces retain contravención or faltas powers, the police-infraction instrument an NGO survey holds responsible for most arrests of trans and travesti people, so documentation gaps in Neuquén do not establish that no exposure exists.

The claim that Law 26.743 is 'no longer guaranteed' rests on activists' assessments reported by the Washington Blade, not on a court finding or a statutory amendment; the statute itself has not been repealed. Whether provincial authorities in Neuquén apply the February 2025 decree or the prison-housing decree as written is not sourced here.
